en: As it was said by the Blessed One:
"If a son of noble family has come with devotion to the teaching of the Sugata,
first the three refuges should be given, and immediately thereafter the thought of awakening."
Immediately after that, having bestowed the five precepts— including the Poṣadha and so forth—
and the renunciation of the ten unwholesome actions, one should make him a lay follower (upāsaka).

As the Blessed One has taught: "If a son of noble family comes with faith toward the teaching of the Sugata, first grant him the three refuges; thereafter, the mind of awakening (bodhicitta). Then, having bestowed the five bases of training, the poṣadha, and so forth, together with the complete abandonment of the ten non-virtues, one should establish him as an upāsaka."
Thus, its sequential order is stated.
The preliminary procedure for this shall now be described.
First, having prepared the guru-maṇḍala according to this sequence: *oṃ vaṃ vajrodake hūṃ svāhā*. With this, the purification of the water is performed.
In that regard, first, one should perform the guru-maṇḍala according to this sequence: *oṃ vaṃ vajrodake hūṃ svāhā*; by this, the water is purified.
Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon birth,
so shall I bathe you with pure, divine water.
Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon their birth, so too do I bathe [you] with the pure waters of the gods.

Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamayaśriye hūṃ. With this, [one performs] the bath. Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā. This is the mantra for washing the hands and feet and sipping water. Oṃ namo bhagavate puṣpaketurājāya tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya. Tadyathā: Oṃ puṣpe puṣpe mahāpuṣpe supuṣpe puṣpodbhave puṣpasaṃbhave puṣpāvakiraṇe svāhā. Thus is the purification of the flowers. Oṃ vajrabhūme hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
With this, one sprinkles water upon the ground: *oṃ vajrasattva sarvavighnān utsāraya hūṃ phaṭ*. With this, one purifies the ground.

oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamayaśriye hūṃ | With this, one performs the ritual bathing. oṃ hrīḥ svāhā | This is the mantra for washing the hands and feet and for the water for the feet. Namo bhagavate puṣpaketurājāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksambuddhāya | tadyathā | oṃ puṣpe puṣpe mahāpuṣpe supuṣpe puṣpodbhave |

With "puṣpa saṃbhava puṣpa āvākirantu svāhā," one should purify the flowers. With "oṃ vajrabhūmi hūṃ phaṭ," one should sprinkle water upon the ground. With "oṃ vajrasattva sarvavighnānutpādaya hūṃ phaṭ," one should purify the ground.
Generosity is cow dung mixed with water; ethical discipline is sweeping; patience is the removal of ants and termites; vigor is the exertion of activity;
meditation is making the mind one-pointed for that moment; and wisdom is the bright, well-drawn lines.
Having constructed the maṇḍala of the Sage, one obtains these very six perfections.

Generosity is the heavy water for bathing, and ethical discipline is the perfect ointment; patience is the removal of tiny gnats, and diligence is the abiding in one's task; meditative concentration is the immediate one-pointedness of mind, and wisdom is the brilliantly blazing painting. By constructing this maṇḍala of the Sage with these six perfections, they shall be attained.
He becomes golden-hued, liberated from all diseases;
golden-hued,
distinguished among gods and men, with a radiant splendor like the moon.
Abundance of wealth and gold arises in the royal lineage of this house of the excellent Sugata by performing physical deeds [of devotion].
Thus is the formation of the mandala.

"By performing physical acts in this supreme palace of the Sugatas, one will be completely liberated from all diseases and attain a golden complexion. One will become exceptionally distinguished among gods and humans, radiant and beautiful like the moon, and possessing an abundance of wealth, gold, and so forth, one will be born into a royal lineage. Thus, one performs the maṇḍala.

Oṃ surekhe vajrarekhe adhiṣṭhantu sarvatathāgatāḥ svāhā. With this, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus in the center of the maṇḍala. Oṃ candrārkavimale svāhā. With this, one should place a single flower in the center of the maṇḍala. Oṃ āḥ hūṃ. With this, one should perform the consecration of body, speech, and mind three times. Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇī mahāpratisare rakṣa 2 māṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ 2 svāhā. With this, one should place a single flower on the head.

Oṃ āsanavajre hūṃ. With this, one should offer a single flower upon the seat. Oṃ suṃ sumerave namaḥ. With this, one should offer a single flower in the center of the maṇḍala. Oṃ haḥ ūrdhvamerave namaḥ; Oṃ hūṃ madhyamerave namaḥ; Oṃ hā adhomerave namaḥ. With these, one offers flowers above, in the middle, and below Mount Meru. Oṃ yaṃ pūrvavidehāya namaḥ. With this, a flower should be offered to the east of Sumeru. Oṃ raṃ jambudvīpāya namaḥ. [Offer] to the south.

Oṃ laṃ, homage to Aparagodānīya; in the west. Oṃ vaṃ, homage to Uttarakuru; in the north. Oṃ yāṃ, homage to the subcontinent [Śāṭhā]; Oṃ rāṃ, homage to the subcontinent [Pūrvavideha]; Oṃ lāṃ, homage to the subcontinent [Jambudvīpa]; Oṃ vāṃ, homage to the subcontinent [Aparagoyānī]. With this, flowers should be offered in the corners beginning with the southeast.
In the [four] corners beginning with the southeast:

*oṃ surekhe vajrakhe ādhitiṣṭhantu sarvatathāgatāḥ svāhā*. With this, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus in the center of the maṇḍala. *oṃ caṇḍākhyavimale svāhā*. With this, one should offer a single flower in the center of the maṇḍala. *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*. With this, one should perform the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the body, speech, and mind three times.

oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa rakṣa māṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā | With this, one offers a flower upon the crown of the head. oṃ āsana-vajre hūṃ | With this, one offers a flower upon the seat. oṃ sumusumeravane namaḥ | With this, one offers a flower in the center of the maṇḍala. oṃ hūṃ auttame ravane namaḥ | oṃ hūṃ madhyame ravane namaḥ |

Oṃ haṃ ādho merave namaḥ: with this, one offers flowers upon, in the middle of, and below Mount Meru. Oṃ yaṃ pūrvavidehāya namaḥ: with this, one offers flowers to the east of Mount Meru. Oṃ raṃ jambudvīpāya namaḥ: [this is] for the south. Oṃ laṃ aparagodānīyāya namaḥ: [this is] for the west. Oṃ vaṃ uttarakuruve namaḥ: [this is] for the north.
oṃ yāḥ aupadvyapāyanamaḥ | oṃ rāḥ aupadvyapāyanamaḥ | oṃ lāḥ aupadvyapāyanamaḥ | oṃ vaṃ aupadvyapāyanamaḥ | With these, one should offer flowers at the corners of the fire and so forth.

Oṃ yaṃ, homage to the elephant-treasure (gajaratna). Oṃ raṃ, homage to the horse-treasure (aśvaratna). Oṃ laṃ, homage to the human-treasure (puruṣaratna). Oṃ vaṃ, homage to the woman-treasure (strīratna). Flowers should be offered within the wombs of Pūrvavideha and the other continents. Oṃ yāḥ, homage to the wheel-treasure (cakraratna). Oṃ rāḥ, homage to the sword-treasure (khaḍgaratna). Oṃ lāḥ, homage to the jewel-treasure (maṇiratna). Oṃ vāḥ, homage to all treasures (sarvanidhāna). Flowers should be offered within the wombs of the corners beginning with the southeast.

Oṃ yāṃ gadgā ratnāya namaḥ | Oṃ rāṃ āśvā ratnāya namaḥ | Oṃ lāṃ pūrūṣa ratnāya namaḥ | Oṃ vāṃ strī ratnāya namaḥ | Offer flowers within the [directions] starting with the east. Oṃ yāḥ cakraratnāya namaḥ | Oṃ yāḥ khaḍgaratnāya namaḥ | Oṃ lāḥ maṇiratnāya namaḥ | Oṃ vāḥ sarvanidhanebhyo namaḥ | Offer flowers within the corners starting with the southeast.

Oṃ āḥ vajragurave idaṃ vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ svāhā. With this, having visualized the Guru as Vajrasattva upon a moon disc on a double-lotus within the interior of the peaked pavilion in the center of Meru, one should offer three handfuls of flowers to the head. Oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajradhūpe hūṃ. Oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajradīpe hūṃ. Oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajragandhe hūṃ. Oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajranaivedye hūṃ.
Whatever else there may be, all that should be offered according to this sequence.

oṃ āḥ vajragurave idaṃ vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ svāhā | With this, one should offer three handfuls of flowers upon the crown of the head to the Guru Vajrasattva, visualized within the central peaked pavilion of Mount Meru, seated upon a variegated lotus and moon disc. oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajradhūpe hūṃ | oṃ āḥ |

Oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajradīpe hūṃ | Oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajragandhe hūṃ | Oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajranṛtye hūṃ | Oṃ āḥ vajragurave vajrādarśanaphalāya hūṃ | By this very sequence, whatever else there may be, all of it should be offered according to this ritual procedure. Thus it is said.
[The Tibetan text is] defiled?
Again, taking a handful of flowers:
Homage to the Buddha, the Guru; homage to the Dharma, the Savior.
Homage to the Sangha; homage always to all three [jewels], however great they may be.
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds;
I rejoice in the merit of the world; I direct my mind toward the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly;
I generate the mind of enlightenment for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others.
I generate the supreme mind of awakening; I invite all sentient beings.
I generate it;
I invite them.
"I shall practice the desired conduct of the excellent path to enlightenment; may I become a Buddha for the benefit of the world."
May I be able to perform the confession of all misdeeds and the rejoicing in all merits.
Having made this declaration, O Noble One, I shall observe the eightfold *poṣadha* fast.
With this verse, "The Noble Eightfold Upoṣadha," one should praise the Guru, who embodies the Three Jewels.

Again, offering with a flower-filled casket: I prostrate to the Buddha, the Sovereign; I prostrate to the Dharma, the Protector; I prostrate to the great Saṅgha. To these three, I constantly prostrate. I take refuge in the Three Jewels. I confess each of my misdeeds. I rejoice in the virtue of all beings. I mentally embrace the awakening of the Buddhas.

In the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly, I take refuge until I reach enlightenment. In order to perfectly accomplish the welfare of myself and others, I shall generate the mind of enlightenment. Having generated the supreme mind of enlightenment, I shall invite all sentient beings as my guests and practice the delightful, sublime conduct of enlightenment.

"May I become a Buddha for the benefit of beings! I shall confess all misdeeds, rejoice in all merit, and having performed these, I shall observe the one-day vows (upoṣadha). This is the noble eight-limbed fast. With this verse, one should offer praise to the Guru, who is the essence of the Three Jewels.
Then,
with a sincere disposition, I offer this complete mandala of jewels to the gurus and the bodhisattvas, for the sake of the world’s attainment of omniscience.
I offer to the giver of the unsurpassed [gift] Mount Meru, consisting of eight peaks, adorned with continents and sub-continents, and endowed with the eight precious gems.
Thus one should offer it.

Then, one should offer [the mandala] to the Gurus and Bodhisattvas with a complete jewel-maṇḍala, offering all things so that beings may attain omniscience. One should make the offering with these words: "I offer to the Unsurpassed Bestower this Mount Meru, possessing eight peaks, adorned with the continents and sub-continents, and perfectly endowed with the eight precious gems. Thus should it be offered.

By the rays of whose grace, those with unclouded vision— having dispelled the darkness by the surrounding radiance of the jewel of their own true nature flashing forth— behold [reality] with great joy.
To that Guru-Bhāskara, this salutation is offered.
Having thus cast the flower, one should perform a prostration.

"I prostrate to that Sun-like Guru, by whose gracious light my own reality was illuminated; having dispelled the darkness with the mass of light from the jewels of reality, those with unimpaired vision look upward and rejoice. Having said this, one should scatter flowers and pay homage.
Thus ends the section on the maṇḍala of the gurus.
Regarding the phrase "the guru-maṇḍala," it refers to the maṇḍala of the guru.

Then, preceded by the recitation of the *gomaya-gāthā*, one should perform three maṇḍalas. Among them, the Buddha-maṇḍala is the maṇḍala with Akṣobhya as the leader, surrounded by Vairocana, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi. The Dharma-maṇḍala is the maṇḍala with the Yoginī-niruttara-tantra as the leader, surrounded by the Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Yoginī tantras.

The Saṅgha-maṇḍala has as its leader Lokeśvara, surrounded by Maitreya, Gaganagañja, Samantabhadra, Vajrapāṇi, Mañjughoṣa, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Kṣitigarbha, and Jñānottara. In these three maṇḍalas, one should offer flowers into the maṇḍala, beginning with the utterance of each individual’s own name and appending the word *namaḥ* at the end, proceeding from the east and circling clockwise.

Proceeding from the east and turning clockwise [319], one should perform the three previous maṇḍalas after reciting the verse beginning with "The gift is heavy. Among these, the maṇḍala in which Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi are accompanied by their retinues, while Akṣobhya is the principal deity, is the Buddha-maṇḍala.

The mandala of the Dharma consists primarily of the Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Yoginī tantras, along with their retinues, and the Unsurpassed Yoga (Anuttarayoga) tantras; [it includes] Maitreya, Gaganagañja, Samantabhadra, and Vajrapāṇi.

Mañjughoṣa, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Kṣitigarbha, and Jñānottara, together with their retinues—centered upon Lokeśvara—constitute the maṇḍala of the Saṅgha. Within these three maṇḍalas, beginning from the east and proceeding clockwise, one should offer flowers into the aforementioned maṇḍala while reciting each of their respective names, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and followed by the sound *namaḥ*.

Having thus constructed the four mandalas according to the sequence described, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family—pure, dressed in clean garments, and at an auspicious lunar day, weekday, and hour—should worship an image of the Tathāgata or others in a pleasing location. Before that [image], preceded by offerings of flowers and so forth according to their means, they should bow to the Three Jewels, worship them as best they can, and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Then, preceded by a handful of flowers, [they should approach] a compassionate and learned guru.
Having prostrated at the feet [of the teacher], and remaining with knees on the ground in a squatting posture or otherwise, with palms joined in reverence, one should thus request three times:
NB: This and the following sections are by Mañjukīrti.

Having thus prepared the four maṇḍalas according to the sequence described, a son or daughter of noble family, endowed with faith, at an auspicious lunar day, weekday, and astrological conjunction, having donned clean and pure garments, should visualize the supreme worship of the Tathāgata’s image—so pleasing to the mind and most excellent—as it is revealed.

Preceded by the offering of flowers and so forth, one should first perform prostrations to the Three Jewels. Likewise, having presented offerings and gifts according to one's ability, one should prostrate at the feet of the Guru—who possesses compassion and omniscience—preceded by the gesture of cupping the hands like a flower-bowl, or else placing the palms joined together at the heart.
Remaining seated cross-legged with palms joined, one should offer this request three times as follows:

"O spiritual friend, please grant me the threefold going for refuge and the generation of the mind of awakening, preceded by the confession of transgressions. Then, having observed that the disciple has acted with resolute intention, the teacher should respond with the words "I grant them according to my ability," and proceed as follows: "Speak, O Long-lived One!"

May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great Bodhisattvas assembled from the world-systems of the ten directions attend to me; may the Preceptor also attend to me. I, who am named so-and-so, whatever evil karma I have committed, caused others to commit, or rejoiced in, having encountered Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, my parents, or other sentient beings through body, speech, or mind—whether in this life or in other previous lives—all that, having gathered it together and condensed it into a single whole, [I confess].

In the presence of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and before my teacher, I confess with the most excellent and sublime teaching. Knowing and remembering, I do not conceal it. Thus three times. [320] All together.
In others... [or] in those others.

"O virtuous spiritual friend, please grant me the confession of misdeeds, the taking of refuge, and the generation of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta). Then, the preceptor, with his superior intention greatly increased, looks upon the disciple and, preceded by the formal commitment to bestow [the vows] as far as he is able, should bestow them in this manner.

O you who possess the gift, speak these words: "May all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, currently residing in all the world-systems of the ten directions, and the great Bodhisattvas, turn their attention toward me; may the Preceptor turn his attention toward me. I, named so-and-so, whatever [merit] I have performed through body, speech, and mind—"

Whatever sinful actions I have committed, caused others to commit, or approved of being committed—either in this life or in infinite other lives—toward the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, my mother and father, or any other sentient beings who have come before me;

Having gathered, combined, totaled, and unified all those instances of mental approval for what was done, I confess and individually acknowledge them in their entirety before the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and my teachers. I shall not conceal them from my knowledge and mindfulness. Thus, three times.

I, [name], who have thus confessed my transgressions, from this day forward until I sit at the seat of enlightenment, go for refuge to the Buddha, the Blessed One—the Great Compassionate One, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing, who has transcended all enmity and fear, the Great Being with an indestructible body, the unsurpassed body, the Dharma-body, the foremost among two-legged beings. I, [name], who have thus confessed my transgressions...

"From this day forward, until I sit at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), I go for refuge to the Dharma—the unsurpassed Great Vehicle, the most excellent among all phenomena. I, who am called by such-and-such a name and have declared myself thus, from this day forward, until I sit at the seat of enlightenment, go for refuge to the Saṅgha of irreversible Bodhisattvas, the tamed, the best among assemblies. Thus three times.

Then, I, who am called [name], having thus confessed my sins, from this day forth until I reach the heart of enlightenment, take refuge in the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—those of great compassion, the omniscient, the all-seeing, those who are everywhere fearless of enemies, the Great Beings, whose bodies are indivisible, whose bodies are unsurpassed.

I take refuge in the Dharmakāya, the supreme among two-legged beings. Then, I, who am called [name], having thus confessed my sins, from this day forward until I reach the heart of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), take refuge in the Dharma—the unsurpassed, most excellent of all dharmas, the Mahāyāna.

Then, I, who am called [name], having thus confessed my misdeeds, from this day forward until I reach the heart of enlightenment, go for refuge to the Sangha of irreversible Bodhisattvas, the most excellent among the assemblies of the disciplined. Thus, three times.

Thus, I, [name], having thus confessed my transgression, from this day forward, having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels, shall generate the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) in order to deliver and uplift the infinite realm of sentient beings, to protect them from the sufferings of *saṃsāra*, and to establish them in the knowledge of the Omniscient One—just as the Buddhas, Blessed Ones, and Great Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, having generated the mind of awakening, have attained, are attaining, and will attain Buddhahood.

Just as all those perfectly awakened ones, with their unobstructed Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-eye, know and see, and having realized the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, grant their approval—by that same method, in the presence of the preceptor named [so-and-so] and before all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, I generate the mind directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. (Recite this three times. [The section on] the supreme extraction of all-knowledge.
[They] know that from this day forward,

until I— whose name is such-and-such— reach the heart of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), I shall go for refuge in the Three [Jewels] in order to definitively deliver and fully liberate the infinite realms of sentient beings, without transgressing these instructions of the preceptor named [so-and-so].

In order to fully protect [beings] from the suffering of saṃsāra and to establish them individually in the wisdom of omniscience, just as the past, future, and present Buddha Bhagavāns and the great Bodhisattvas have generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) for enlightenment;

For the sake of the Buddhas, they have gone forth, are going forth, and will go forth; and just as all those Perfectly Enlightened Ones have known and seen with unobstructed Buddha-wisdom and the Buddha-eye, so too [should it be understood].

Just as you have known and directly realized the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, by that very same ritual procedure, I, who am called [name], shall generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) in the presence of the preceptor and before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Thus, three times.
From this day forward, may all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as my preceptor, regard me as a Bodhisattva.
"From this day forward," [the Buddha said],
"I pray that all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Teacher may take me, as a Bodhisattva, under their care."
Thus is the taking of refuge in the Three Jewels, preceded by the generation of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).
By taking refuge in the Three Jewels, one first generates the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
The undertaking of the five precepts constitutes the lay follower's vow; it should be conferred in this manner upon a disciple who has made the formal request.
Furthermore, when one who is a lay follower (upāsaka) undertaking the five precepts makes a formal request, it should be granted for the sake of the disciple in this manner:

Speak, venerable one; attend to it, Preceptor: just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, have abstained from the taking of life—even so I, [name], from this day forward for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, shall abstain from the taking of life. By this first limb, I train after the training of those noble Arhats; I conform to it; I imitate it.

"Venerable one, speak thus: 'O Teacher, please attend to me! Just as those noble Arhats, for as long as they live, have abandoned taking life and abstained from taking life, so too shall I, who am called [name], from this time forward, [abstain from taking life]...'"

"For as long as I live, I shall abstain from taking life and turn away from killing. By this first limb, I shall train in accordance with the training of those noble Arhats; I shall practice it and follow it."

Furthermore: Pay attention, Preceptor! Just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, have abstained from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants; [so may you do].

[124] Likewise, I, named so-and-so, from this day forward for as long as life lasts, having abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants—abstaining from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants—I, by means of this fifth limb, train in accordance with, conform to, and imitate the training of those noble Arhats.
"And may the Teacher accept me as a lay follower. Thus a second and a third time.

Furthermore, Master, please listen: Just as those noble Arhats have, for as long as they live, abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, speaking falsehoods, and the consumption of fermented grain-liquor and distilled liquors which cause intoxication and heedlessness—namely, taking what is not given and sexual misconduct—[so too should one do so].

Just as one has desisted from speaking falsehoods and from the consumption of fermented grain liquor and distilled spirits—which cause intoxication and are the basis for heedlessness—so too, I, who am called [name], from this day forward for as long as I live, shall likewise abstain from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, speaking falsehoods, and fermented grain liquor.

I shall desist from fermented liquor and spirits that cause intoxication and heedlessness. By these five limbs, I follow the training of those noble Arhats; I shall practice it and perform it accordingly. May the Master accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka). This is repeated a second and a third time.

If one now wishes to perform the Noble Eightfold Poṣadha, then, as before, after granting the three refuges to the disciple who has made the request, the eight precepts should be conferred in this manner:

Speak, O Venerable One, attend to me, Teacher: I, named so-and-so, from this moment until the coming night, and until the rising of the sun tomorrow—during this interval, I abstain from the killing of all living beings, from taking what belongs to others, from unchaste conduct, as well as from divisive speech, falsehoods that produce intoxication, drinking [liquor], eating at improper times, from the use of garlands, ointments, dancing, singing, and amusements, and from high beds and seats; today I abstain from these and adopt the conduct of the Arhats through its eight virtues.
Three times in this manner.

[One] who wishes to perform the *poṣadha* endowed with the eight branches of the noble ones should, at that time, first make a formal request as before; then, for the sake of the disciple, these eight points—blessed by the taking of refuge in the Three [Jewels]—should be granted as follows: "Venerable one, you must say this: 'Teacher, please attend to me.'"

I, who am called [name], from this time forth until the end of the night and until the rising of the sun, shall refrain from all taking of life, from seizing the wealth of others, from unchaste conduct, from speaking falsehoods arising from divisive speech, from intoxicants that cause heedlessness, and from eating at improper times.

"From this day forward, I shall abandon delight in social gatherings, in [excessive] dress, in dancing, singing, instrumental music, and flirtatious gestures, and in high beds and seats; for I am entering upon the eight qualities of an Arhat. Likewise, he should repeat this three times:

"This is my undertaking of the Poṣadha vows and restraint for the adornment of the mind, for the equipment of the mind, and for the attainment of the fruit of the unsurpassed knowledge of all sentient beings. Then the teacher should say, "It is appropriate," and the disciple should say, "Excellent."

"I have correctly undertaken this undertaking of the *poṣadha* ethical discipline for the sake of adorning the mind, for the equipment of the mind, and for the purpose of attaining the fruit of unsurpassed primordial wisdom (*anuttara-jñāna*) for all sentient beings. Then the preceptor should say, "This is the means," and the student should say, "Excellent!"
Because it nourishes all that is wholesome and purifies the evil committed here in this world,
through that nourishment and the purification of the mind, it is called "nourishment" (puṣṭi).
The Tathāgata said, "It is the Poṣadha."
Thus ends the procedure for the Poṣadha ceremony.

Because it nourishes all virtues without exception and purifies the accumulated sins here, that which both nourishes and thoroughly purifies was called "poṣadha" (the nourishing purification) by the Tathāgata. This is the ritual for the poṣadha.
This very restraint belongs to the owner of the cow. || O ||
"This very [discipline] is the vow that leads to restraint," it is said.
